title: AI can generate 100 trading strategies before you've properly tested one. How do you avoid overfitting?
author: criticized_Egg
selftext:
I spent quite a while building a Python quant research project, and the hardest part wasn't writing strategies. It was figuring out whether any of the results actually meant something.

If you test enough variations, something will eventually look promising. Add unrealistic fills, underestimated costs or accidentally using future information, and it's even easier to fool yourself.

I never managed to validate a profitable strategy, so I decided to open-source the useful research tooling instead.

It includes backtesting code, explicit execution assumptions, offline demos and documented negative results. It's not an AI strategy generator or a live trading bot.

GitHub: [https://github.com/privEgem/open-quant-trading-lab](https://github.com/privEgem/open-quant-trading-lab)

For those using AI agents to generate and test strategies, how do you track all the attempts and keep your test data genuinely untouched?

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
respect for open-sourcing the tooling and the negatives instead of pretending something worked. that's rarer than an actual edge around here.



on your question, here's what ended up working for me after a lot of fooling myself:



1. every idea goes in a ledger before it's tested, including the ones the AI suggests and I drop after a quick look. it's just a text file with an ID, the date, the hypothesis and the outcome. the number of rows is the number that matters. if it says 40, a t-stat of 2.5 on the winner means nothing, since the best of 40 random strategies hits about that on luck alone.



2. the rule gets written and saved before any data is touched. entry, exit, costs, which period, and what result counts as a pass. I hash the file so I can't quietly edit it later. any change after that is a new attempt and goes in the ledger.



3. the date lock lives in the code, not in my head. the loader filters out the test period before anything else reads the data, and every run prints the min and max dates it actually loaded. one thing I learned the hard way: if an AI agent can download its own data, your "locked" period isn't locked.



4. for anything an LLM came up with, I assume it has already seen the history before its training cutoff. so for those ideas only data after the cutoff, or forward results, counts as a real test.



5. the final holdout gets read once. if it fails, the idea is dead. no "let me just adjust one thing and rerun".



honestly the ledger alone changed more for me than any fancy statistic. once you see the real count written down, it gets a lot harder to get excited about a single nice backtest.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
you open-sourced the negative results after the mltraders thread, so you already do the hard half. for the agent case, two things I'd insist on.

the agent never gets the test data. not as a line in the prompt, the file just isn't on the machine it runs on. it submits a rule, a separate job scores it on the held-out years and hands back one line. if it can read the rows it will end up tuned to them, without anyone meaning it.

every submission is logged before the score comes back, with a hash of the rule. then the number of attempts is a fact and you can discount the best result by it. 100 tries at a 5% bar gives about five that pass on noise alone, so a survivor has to beat the best of 100 shuffled runs, not zero.

the leak that's left is you. once you see a held-out score and go back to edit, that data is spent. keep one last slice that nobody opens until the end, you included.
